To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we detected the diffuse interstellar band (DIB) features in the optical spectra from 11 starburst galaxies and (2) we found that the relative strengths of these features are very similar in starbursts and the diffuse interstellar medium of our Galaxy.
the DIB features in starbursts are very similar to those in the Milky Way.

the DIB properties in starbursts are surprisingly similar to those in the diffuse ISMs of the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds, despite their much higher photon and cosmic-ray fluxes, and that this "homology" can help explain the similarities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of the DIBs, the study of the physical properties of the gas in which they are found, and the search for a chemical explanation of their origins.
the study of the interstellar medium (ISM) in the most powerful starburst galaxies in the local Universe.
understanding the physical processes that give rise to DIBs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DIBs are ubiquitous, and are found in a wide range of environments, and that the DIB carriers are likely to be present in the interstellar medium in all galaxies.
the DIB carriers in the starburst galaxies are the same as those found in the diffuse interstellar medium of our own Galaxy.

, at the current stage, the DIBs are detected in starbursts, and the DIBs detected in starburst galaxies are similar to DIBs in the Milky Way, but we do not know if they are produced by the same molecules, and if they are produced at all by the same mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DIB carriers are not destroyed by the harsh conditions in intense starbursts.
the DIB-producing gas in starbursts appears to be a scaled-up analog of the diffuse intercloud gas in the Milky Way.
the DIB carriers are not sensitive to the extreme radiation fields found in starburst galaxies.
The main takeaway from our work is that

DIB-producing gas is ubiquitous in dusty starbursts, and that the DIB properties in these intense starburst environments are very similar to those in the diffuse ISMs of the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds.
DIBs can survive in the harsh conditions of intense starbursts.
the DIB carriers in the ISM are remarkably robust against the harsh conditions of starbursts, surviving the intense radiation field and high gas densities.
